409.t: Joining Duke and learning the plunger from Tricky Sam
409.s: Hired to play Bubber Miley's plunger role, he had never used one and learned it by listening to Tricky Sam Nanton.
409.q: And so I left and went up there with Duke. And I said -- I used to laugh when Tricky would start to blowing, you know. It sounded funny to me.

409.s: The plunger was Bubber Miley's trademark that Cootie learned from Tricky Sam; his own open style came from Louis Armstrong.
409.q: Yeah, it did become a part of me, because that was what Duke Ellington hired me to do. And it dawned on me. 89.t: Charlie Irvis, Bubber Miley and the New York origin of the growl
89.s: The five-piece band added trombonist Charlie Irvis, who invented the growl on trombone, and Bubber Miley; both were New Yorkers.
89.q: Five pieces when they were at the Kentucky Club. Yes, five pieces. Then they added on a trombone player name of Charlie Irvis who did the plunger bit, the Tricky Sam, he created that. 89.t: King Oliver at the Dreamland and where the growl came from
89.s: On tour with Mamie Smith in Chicago he and Bubber Miley nightly heard King Oliver's mute growl, which Bubber brought to Ellington.
